TAGLINE: The hip ballgame of Mexico, as it is played.
MENU_QUICK_DESC: Pick a court and two towns. Play now.
MENU_CUP_DESC: Eight towns, knock-out, to the final.
MENU_WATCH_DESC: Two towns, played by the computer.
MENU_HOWTO_DESC: The rules, the count and the story.
MENU_FOOT: Ulama de cadera, the living hip game of Sinaloa, and the classic stone court, reconstructed.
RULES_NOTE_ULAMA: Ulama de cadera as it is played in southern Sinaloa today: hip strikes only, the ball must cross the analco, and the count of rayas swings up and down to eight.
RULES_NOTE_CLASSIC: A reconstruction of the old stone-court game from the chroniclers: points to eight, the ball plays off the sloped walls, and the ball through a ring wins outright. Very rare.
LENGTH_NOTE: Real ulama games run until a side reaches eight rayas, and can last a long time. With a time limit, the side holding the count when time is up wins; if the count is level, the next raya wins.
DIFF_VILLAGE_DESC: They read the ball slowly and their strikes go astray.
DIFF_REGIONAL_DESC: Good timing, deep returns, the odd low skidding ball.
DIFF_CHAMPION_DESC: Quick to the ball, clean hips, low hard returns you must dive for.

CUP_INTRO: Eight towns are drawn into a knock-out: quarter-finals, semi-finals and the final. Win and go on; lose and you are out. Choose the game and your town.
CUP_KIND_ULAMA: On the earth courts of Sinaloa.
CUP_OUT: Your town is out. The tournament plays on to its final.
RULES_AIM_TEXT: Two sides strike a heavy rubber ball back and forth across the middle of a long court, with the hips. The side that fails to return it loses a raya. The first side to eight rayas wins.
RULES_COURT_TEXT: Ulama is played on the taste, a strip of packed earth about 60 metres long and 4 wide, with no walls. The analco is the line across its middle; the chivo is the end line at each end. Each side stays in its own half.
RULES_BALL_TEXT: Solid natural rubber, about 3.6 kg and under 20 cm across. It is heavy: it flies low, thuds down, hardly bounces on earth, and soon stops rolling.
RULES_HIP_TEXT: The ball is struck with the hip and nothing else. Players turn side-on, sink low and swing the hip into it. For a low or rolling ball they go down to the ground and meet it with the hip there. Teammates may play it on in turn.
RULES_RAYA_TEXT: A raya goes to the other side when the ball dies in your half (it did not cross the analco), when it goes past your end line, when your strike sends it out at the side, or when it touches one of you anywhere but the hip.
RULES_COUNT_TEXT: Only one side holds the count at a time. A raya to the side holding it adds one. A raya to the other side takes one off; at level, the next raya starts that side's count. The count swings up and down until a side reaches eight.
RULES_URRIA_TEXT: On certain rayas the side holding the count is in urria, in danger: if it loses the next raya, its whole count is wiped out. Villages place urria differently; the game uses rayas 3 and 7 unless you choose otherwise.
RULES_FAULTS_TEXT: Hands, feet, knees or body: any touch but the hip is a fault, and the raya goes to the other side. So is knocking the ball out at the side. Stand out of its way if you are not striking it.
RULES_SERVE_TEXT: The server, the male, puts the ball in play by hand across the analco: rolled along the earth (male abajo) or thrown high (male arriba). In the game it rolls from level and is thrown when a side holds the count; the side that won the last raya serves.
RULES_TIME_TEXT: Real games run until a side reaches eight. If you set a time limit, the side holding the count when it runs out wins; if the count is level, the next raya wins.
RULES_CLASSIC_TEXT: The stone court is shaped like an I: an alley between sloped walls, with an end court at each end. Following the old chronicles, a point is won when the ball dies in the other half, lands in their end court, or touches them anywhere but the hip. Points to eight. The rules of the old game are not fully known: this is a reconstruction.
RULES_RING_TEXT: A stone ring is set high in each wall at the middle of the alley. The chroniclers wrote that the ball through a ring won the game outright, and that it very seldom happened. It takes a clean, high strike near the middle, aimed along the wall.
CTRL_MOVE_TEXT: Your left thumb, anywhere on the left of the screen, is a joystick. You play the one of your side who goes for the ball; the game switches to him.
CTRL_HIP_TEXT: The hip strike. Tap it just before the ball reaches your hip: the swing takes a quarter of a second. Early or late, the ball goes weakly or astray, or hits your body.
CTRL_DIVE_TEXT: Down on the ground to meet a low or rolling ball with your hip.
CTRL_AIM_TEXT: Hold the joystick as you strike: toward their end for a long high ball, back toward yours for a low hard one that skids along the earth, across for that side. With no thumb on it, you send it where your teammates would.
CTRL_SERVE_TEXT: When your side serves, tap SERVE.
CTRL_READ_TEXT: The ball's shadow on the earth shows how high it is. A pale ring marks where it will come down to hip height in your half.
CTRL_ASSIST_TEXT: With help on (Settings), your player goes to meet the ball whenever your thumb is off the joystick: the timing is up to you.
CTRL_KEYS_TEXT: WASD or the arrows to move, Space for the first button, J for the second, Esc to pause.
SIG_RAYA_TEXT: Two judges, the veedores, stand at the analco. For each raya they point to the half of the side that wins it, and the call is shown at the top of the screen.
SIG_FAULT_TEXT: For a fault (a touch that was not the hip, the ball out at the side) they cross their arms over their heads, then point.
SIG_COUNT_TEXT: The board at the top keeps the count in rayas, tally strokes, filled in the colour of the side holding the count, from its end.
SIG_URRIA_TEXT: The urria rayas are marked under the board; the mark turns red while the side holding the count stands on one.
STORY_OLD_TEXT: People in Mesoamerica have played with rubber balls for over three thousand years; more than two thousand ball courts are known. The Classic Maya called the game pitz. In Nahuatl it was ōllamaliztli, from ōlli, rubber, and the court was tlachtli.
STORY_ULAMA_TEXT: Ulama, from ōllamaliztli, is still played in villages of southern Sinaloa, Mexico, by a few families and teams who keep it alive. Hip ulama is played on the taste with a ball of three to four kilograms.
STORY_REVIVAL_TEXT: In the Yucatán, Quintana Roo, Belize, Guatemala and Honduras, teams have revived the game as pok-ta-pok or pelota maya, with an international championship held since 2015. Each tournament sets its own rules.
STORY_WORDS_TEXT: Pok-ta-pok was coined in 1932 from the Yucatec Maya word pokolpok. Raya, taste, analco, chivo, male and urria are the words of the Sinaloa game.
STORY_RESPECT_TEXT: The ballgame is a living tradition of Indigenous and Mexican communities. This game tries to show it as it is played; the people who play it are its keepers. Names of towns are used as place names only; the teams and players are invented.
MOVE_BUTTONS_NOTE: Drag each button where your thumb wants it. Your places are kept for every match.
ASSIST_ON_NOTE: Your player goes to meet the ball when your thumb is off the joystick. The timing of the strike is yours.
SET_COACH_NOTE: Short tips during your first match. They turn off by themselves after it.
GFX_NOTE: Low suits phones with little memory; High adds shadows and finer light.
